findings.quote: The thing to watch is the few seconds before the health checks notice.
findings.type: technical: wrong or unsupported quantity in a spoken answer
findings.evidence: Facts elb-alb-unhealthy-threshold-default-2 ("2 consecutive failed health checks") and elb-alb-health-check-interval-default-30-seconds ("30 seconds"): with the defaults that the chapter itself puts in its A-list, a failed target is detected after two checks 30 seconds apart, so about a minute, not a few seconds. The linked fact ec2-auto-scaling-faq-elb-requests-before-detection-fail says some requests fail before detection, but it gives no duration. The script tells a CEO about a gap that is several times shorter than the default. findings.section: a-load-balancer-gives-each-enabled-availability-zone-its-own-node (Go deeper: subnets and more than one Region)
findings.quote: [Avoid creating empty subnets](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-empty-subnet-503): an empty zone [triggers 503 errors for HTTP requests](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-empty-subnet-503).
findings.type: technical: condition dropped from a fact
findings.evidence: source_id docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/edit-target-group-attributes: the sentence stands in the best-practice list for target groups with cross-zone load balancing turned off. The bullet above it says: "This is to avoid an Availability Zone being empty while cross-zone load balancing is off, as this triggers a 503 error for all HTTP requests that enter the empty Availability Zone." The same section starts: "With Application Load Balancers, cross-zone load balancing is always turned on at the load balancer level". The chapter teaches that ALB cross-zone is on by default (elb-alb-cross-zone-on-by-default), so the reader will think that any zone without targets returns 503 errors, which is the default case only when cross-zone is turned off for the target group. The fact claim of elb-alb-empty-subnet-503 drops the condition too: amend its qualifiers.condition to "cross-zone load balancing turned off for the target group", and add "when cross-zone load balancing is off" to the sentence.
findings.resolution: fix-14: the condition is in the sentence: 'With cross-zone load balancing turned off for a target group, [avoid creating empty subnets]: DNS still gives out their zonal addresses, which [triggers 503 errors for HTTP requests].' Condition checked in the saved snapshot (search: 'being empty while cross-zone load balancing is off', edit-target-group-attributes line 308). The fact itself is not amended here: an amend changes rev, drops the verified status until new votes, and resets every dependent item; the qualifier change is reported to the registrar.

findings.quote: 3. **Terminate on the NLB.** A TLS listener ends TLS on the NLB, and the [source IP continues to be preserved](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-faq-source-ip-preserved-with-tls). / FAQ 6. Does an NLB keep the client IP when it terminates TLS? Yes.
findings.type: technical: contradicts the chapter's own table; condition missing
findings.evidence: Fact elb-nlb-client-ip-preservation-defaults (source_id docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/load-balancer-target-groups): "The default is disabled if the target group type is IP address and the target group protocol is TCP or TLS. Otherwise, the default is enabled." The chapter's own table in the NLB subsection says "NLB, IP targets with TCP or TLS | Not by default". The FAQ sentence is unconditional, and the chapter repeats it without the condition, so the two places give opposite answers for IP targets (for example containers with awsvpc networking). Fix: keep the FAQ quote, but add the condition in both places, for example "with instance targets, or with client IP preservation turned on for IP targets".
findings.resolution: fix-14: step 3 now reads 'A TLS listener ends TLS on the NLB. With instance targets, the [source IP continues to be preserved]; for IP targets with TLS, [the default is disabled](elb-nlb-client-ip-preservation-defaults).' FAQ 6 now asks 'Does an NLB with instance targets keep the client IP when it terminates TLS?' and keeps the verbatim FAQ quote.

findings.quote: 3. **Match.** A rule matches on [host-header](...), [path-pattern](...), [query-string](...) or [source-ip](...).
findings.type: claims: list reads as complete; fact has more
findings.evidence: Fact elb-alb-condition-types (source_id docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-condition-types): "Each rule can optionally include zero or one of each of the following conditions: `host-header`, `http-request-method`, `path-pattern`, and `source-ip`. Each rule can also include zero or more of each of the following conditions: `http-header` and `query-string`." The sentence leaves out http-header and http-request-method, and exam stems do route by header (for example a mobile User-Agent). Fix: "for example on host-header, path-pattern, http-header, query-string or source-ip".
findings.resolution: fix-14: step 3 now reads 'A rule matches, for example, on [host-header], [path-pattern], [query-string], [source-ip] or an HTTP header.' The links all go to elb-alb-condition-types, whose claim names HTTP headers.

findings.quote: 4. **Act.** The rule forwards, returns a fixed response, or redirects, for example from [HTTP to HTTPS](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-redirect-http-to-https).
findings.type: claims: unsupported list without a fact link; omits authentication actions
findings.evidence: source_id docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/rule-action-types lists `authenticate-cognito`, `authenticate-oidc`, `fixed-response`, `forward`, `jwt-validation` and `redirect`, and says: "Each rule must include exactly one of the following routing actions: `forward`, `redirect`, or `fixed-response`, and it must be the last action to be performed." The sentence is true only for the routing actions, and the link supports only the redirect example. findings.resolution: fix-14: step 4 now says 'The routing action forwards, returns a fixed response, or redirects ... An HTTPS listener rule can add [a user authentication action and a routing action](elb-alb-action-types-list). Users then sign in through an [OpenID Connect (OIDC) compliant](elb-alb-user-authentication-idps) provider or Amazon Cognito.' Card elb-c032 now has teaching text behind it.

findings.quote: You can [optionally associate one Elastic IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip) per subnet.
findings.type: technical: condition dropped from a fact
findings.evidence: Fact elb-nlb-static-ip-per-az-optional-eip (source_id docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works): "You can optionally associate one Elastic IP address with each network interface when you create the Network Load Balancer." findings.quote: Yes. Target logs [only contain the IP address](../facts/elb.md#elb-alb-xff-holds-client-ip) of the load balancer, and the VPC rule allows it.
findings.type: claims: link does not support the sentence
findings.evidence: Fact elb-alb-xff-holds-client-ip quotes: "Because load balancers intercept traffic between clients and servers, your server access logs only contain the IP address of the load balancer." It is about what the server logs show, not about the source address of the packets that a security group rule checks. The answer needs: the load balancer reaches targets from private addresses in its own subnets (fact elb-node-sends-to-target-private-ip, "using its private IP address"), and those addresses are inside the VPC range. Fix: cite elb-node-sends-to-target-private-ip and drop the log fact here.
findings.resolution: fix-14: the answer now reads 'Yes. The load balancer reaches its targets [using private IP addresses](elb-targets-need-no-public-ip) inside the VPC, so the VPC rule allows them.' The log fact is gone. elb-node-sends-to-target-private-ip was not used: its 'its private IP address' is the target's address (the destination), so elb-targets-need-no-public-ip ('route requests to your targets using private IP addresses') fits better.

findings.quote: | One appliance fails | It [reroutes traffic to a healthy appliance instance](...) | / | Existing flows, default setting | It will [send existing flows to the same target](...) |
findings.type: technical: two rows give opposite gists
findings.evidence: Fact elb-gwlb-target-failover-default-no-rebalance claims: "By default (no_rebalance), a Gateway Load Balancer keeps sending existing flows to a target that has failed or been deregistered, while new flows go to healthy targets". Row 1 reads as if all traffic moves at once, and row 2 says existing flows stay. A reader who reads only the table (READER.md: she trusts the gist of one glance) gets a contradiction. Fix row 1: "New flows go to a healthy appliance", and keep row 2.
findings.resolution: fix-14: row 1 is now 'One appliance fails: new flows | Go to a healthy appliance: [new flows are sent to healthy targets]' and row 2 'One appliance fails: existing flows, default setting | It will [send existing flows to the same target]', both linked to elb-gwlb-target-failover-default-no-rebalance.

findings.section: elb-t02 step 6 (break_it); 2-deep.md listener-rules subsection (Try it callout)
findings.quote: Route one path with a listener rule, then add a catch-all rule with a lower priority number and watch it win.
findings.type: technical: a break-it step that cannot fail and does not show the behavior
findings.evidence: Rule broken: TOOLS-items.md 8.3, "A break-it step must fail; every other command must return 0." In elb-t02 the break_it step is `aws elbv2 describe-rules ...`, a read that succeeds whatever the rule order is. The load balancer is internal, so CloudShell sends no request to it, and the reader never sees a request get "catch-all". She only reads the priorities and is told the result in the explain text. The callout promises "watch it win". Fix: either reword the callout and the step ("read the order and predict which rule wins") and set break_it on no read step, or add a step that observes the effect safely (for example a CloudShell VPC environment in the default VPC that runs curl against the internal DNS name) with an expect that can fail.
findings.resolution: fix-14: first option taken. elb-t02 step 6 is no longer a break-it step: its text asks the reader to predict first, and its expect gives the answer (the listener checks the lowest priority number first, so /api/orders gets catch-all). Title now 'Route by path with listener rules and predict the rule order'; the 2-deep Try it callout now says '... and predict which rule wins.' Commands unchanged (the CLI report still matches). The chapter keeps its required break-it step in elb-t03 (tasks lint --ship clean).

The spec notes of diagrams/src/elb-hero.json name step facts (elb-dns-returns-node-ips, elb-listener-checks-connection-requests, elb-alb-rules-priority-then-algorithm, elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume), but only step 4 carries a link. findings.quote: the duration-based cookie fits an application without its own session cookie.
findings.type: technical: explanation adds a condition that the stem does not give
findings.evidence: Fact elb-alb-sticky-duration-vs-application-cookie: "use application-based stickiness when the application has its own session cookie, and duration-based stickiness when it does not." The stem only says that the application keeps each user's session data in the memory of one instance. It never says whether the application sets its own session cookie, and such an application usually does. The chapter's card elb-c022 teaches the application-based answer for that case. The key works because no option offers application-based stickiness, but the Why teaches a reason that the stem does not support. Fix: add "The application sets no cookie of its own" to the stem, or change the Why to say that both cookie types bind the user and only the duration-based one is offered.
findings.resolution: fix-14: explanation only (stem, options and key unchanged, so the passed verification stands): the clause now reads '... both kinds send a user back to one target, and the duration-based kind needs no cookie from the application.' The unsupported stem assumption is gone; q lint clean.

findings.section: changed-recently (1-fast.md) and the A-list Changed recently entry (2-deep.md)
findings.quote: > **Changed recently:** (2025-02-13) A Network Load Balancer can remove an Availability Zone.
findings.type: claims: changes since 2022 that the chapter does not mention
findings.evidence: source_id docs/elasticloadbalancing/latest/network/doc-history lists, before the 2026-07-15 cutoff: "This release adds support for QUIC and TCP\_QUIC protocols." (November 13, 2025), "This release adds support for default action with weighted target groups." Nothing in the chapter is wrong because of these changes, but the sentence "Its rules choose a target group" and the NLB listener list (claims-05) are now ALB-only or incomplete.
